rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Probability quantifies chance: **P(A) = m/n** on equally likely outcomes, bounded by the axioms with the **complement law** P(A) + P(A′) = 1 powering the "at least one = 1 − none" shortcut. The **addition law** P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B) subtracts the double-counted overlap (NEB 2022: 0.6 + 0.5 − 0.3 = **0.8**), collapsing to a sum only for mutually exclusive events — which are emphatically **not** independent.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - P(A) = m/n; P(A′) = 1 − P(A) - P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B); exclusive: P(A) + P(B) - P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B); P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B|A) - Bayes: P(Aᵢ|B) = P(Aᵢ)P(B|Aᵢ)/Σⱼ P(Aⱼ)P(B|Aⱼ)

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The deck remembers*** — without replacement the second draw is conditional on the first (3/9 after a red); with replacement it is independent (4/10 again).

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Arithmetic of Chance Probability measures uncertainty on a 0–1 scale. The theorem set: the **classical (Laplace) definition** m/n, the **addition law** with the mutually-exclusive special case, the **conditional probability** P(A|B), the **multiplication law**, **independence**, and **Bayes' theorem**.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Classical definition and its axioms - **P(A) = m/n**: m favourable outcomes among n equally likely ones. - **Axioms:** 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1; P(φ) = 0; P(S) = 1; and P(A) + P(A′) = **1** (the complement law — the "at least one" workhorse: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none)). ### 2.2 Addition law - **Theorem:** P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B) — the overlap counted twice must be subtracted once.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: At least one: 1 - P(none). King or heart: add then subtract the overlap. Both-red without replacement: multiply conditionals. Bayes: prior x likelihood over total probability.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB 2022 (verified PYQ): If P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A∩B) = 0.3, then P(A∪B) is: (1m)** — **Addition law:** P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B) — the intersection must be subtracted because the individual probabilities count it twice. **Substitute:** P(A∪B) = 0.6 + 0.5 − 0.3 = **0.8**.…  ·  **NEB-style (3m): A bag contains 4 red and 6 black balls. Two balls are drawn one after the other without replacement. Find the probability that both are red.** — **Case named:** without replacement ⟹ conditional (the deck remembers). **Step 1:** P(first red) = 4/10 = 2/5.…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Name the case (with/without replacement, exclusive/independent) before computing - the naming is the method mark.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: The complement trick converts "at least one" questions into one subtraction; Bayes converts evidence about effects back into probabilities of causes.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Classical definition: P(A) = m/n for equally likely outcomes. Axioms: 0 <= P <= 1; P(S) = 1; complement law P(A) + P(A') = 1, so P(at least one) = 1 - P(none). Addition law: P(A u B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A n B); mutually exclusive case drops the intersection. Conditional probability: P(A|B) = P(A n B)/P(B).…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Medical screening misleads intuition precisely because P(positive | disease) and P(disease | positive) differ - Bayes' theorem is the correction.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: **NEB-style (2m): One card is drawn from a well-shuffled pack of 52. Find the probability that it is a king or a heart.** — **Sets:** kings (4 cards), hearts (13 cards), and their intersection (king of hearts, 1 card). **Addition law:** P(king ∪ heart) = 4/52 + 13/52 − 1/52 = 16/52 = **4/13**.…  ·  **NEB-style (3m): Machine A produces 60% of a factory's items with 2% defective rate; machine B produces 40% with 5% defective rate. An item chosen at random is found defective.…

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 3. Scientific Definitions | Term | Scientific meaning | Example | |---|---|---| | **Sample space S** | Set of all outcomes | two dice: 36 ordered pairs | | **Mutually exclusive** | A∩B = φ | head and tail on one toss | | **Conditional probability** | P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) | draw given a red came first | | **Independent events** | P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) | two separate coins |  ·  ## 4. Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 The complement trick - "At least one success" is the complement of "no successes". Counting at-least-one directly is error-prone; 1 − P(none) is one line. The single most useful probability shortcut. ### 4.2 With and without replacement - Without replacement, the second draw's probability is **conditional** — the deck remembers.…  ·  ## 5. Comparison Tables **Key distinctions** | Pair | Difference | |---|---| | exclusive vs independent | exclusive: cannot co-occur; independent: no influence | | P(A|B) vs P(B|A) | different conditionals; Bayes converts between them | | with vs without replacement | independent vs conditional draws |

rows.text: A king or a heart is drawn from 52 cards - find the probability.  ·  State the limit / condition where a formula or rule stops being valid before applying it.  ·  Limit to remember: p(e) = favourable/total. additive law: p(a∪b) = p(a)+p(b)−p(a∩b). if mutually exclusive, p(a∪b)=p(a)+p(b).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ## 6. Common Confusions **Mutually exclusive ≠ independent:** if A and B are exclusive and P(A), P(B) > 0, then P(A∩B) = 0 ≠ P(A)P(B) — exclusive events are maximally dependent.  ·  **Addition law needs the overlap:** forgetting −P(A∩B) overcounts; only the exclusive case drops it.  ·  **P(A|B) ≠ P(B|A):** the probability of disease given a positive test is not the test's accuracy — Bayes exists because these differ.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ## 7. Exam Application **NEB 2022 (verified PYQ): If P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A∩B) = 0.3, then P(A∪B) = ? (1m)** — Addition law: P(A∪B) = 0.6 + 0.5 − 0.3 = **0.8**. Note P(A∩B) = 0.3 ≠ P(A)P(B) = 0.30...…  ·  **NEB-style (3m): A bag contains 4 red and 6 black balls. Two balls are drawn one after the other without replacement. Find the probability that both are red.** — **Conditional multiplication:** P(1st red) = 4/10; P(2nd red | 1st red) = 3/9. P(both red) = (4/10)(3/9) = **12/90 = 2/15**.…  ·  **NEB-style (2m): A card is drawn from a pack of 52. Find the probability that it is a king or a heart.** — P(king) = 4/52; P(heart) = 13/52; P(king ∩ heart) = 1/52 (the king of hearts is counted twice otherwise). Addition law: 4/52 + 13/52 − 1/52 = **16/52 = 4/13**.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **NEB-style (3m): In a factory, machine A produces 60% of items with 2% defectives, machine B 40% with 5% defectives. An item is found defective. Find the probability it came from A. (Bayes)** — P(defective) = (0.6)(0.02) + (0.4)(0.05) = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032 (total probability).…
